lessons.body:
Threat Model and Security Baseline
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Start from assets and abuse cases
TaskFlow threat-model loop

Asset                     Entry point              Abuse case                    Control
what matters?               where input enters        how it can fail           prevent / detect

Then test the control and log enough to investigate failures.

TaskFlow protects authentication sessions, tenant-scoped business data, attachments, authorization
decisions, secrets, audit evidence and service availability. Threat modeling asks how each can be read,
changed, destroyed or abused.

Representative abuse cases
• Attacker reuses a stolen access token.

• MEMBER changes an ID and attempts to read another Workspace.

• Bot brute-forces auth endpoints or floods expensive list/search routes.

• Malicious description tries to become executable HTML.

• Uploaded PDF is disguised executable/active content.

• Service-role key leaks into browser bundle or logs.

• Proxy misconfiguration makes all clients appear to have the same IP.

• Dependency vulnerability remains unpatched despite a released security fix.

Baseline
Use OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 as a verification catalog, not as a checkbox trophy. TaskFlow selects requirements
relevant to its architecture and records evidence in tests/configuration.

lessons.body:
Rate Limiting and Abuse Controls
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Use rate limits as one control
ThrottlerModule.forRoot([
{ name: "short", ttl: 1_000, limit: 10 },
{ name: "minute", ttl: 60_000, limit: 120 },
])

// bind ThrottlerGuard globally; override tighter on expensive/auth routes

Choose a tracker intentionally
• Behind a trusted proxy/load balancer, configure trust proxy correctly before trusting forwarded IP
information.

• For authenticated endpoints, user ID can be part of abuse policy in addition to IP.

• One in-memory limiter is only instance-local; multi-replica deployments require a shared store or
upstream gateway limiter.

• 429 is a capacity/abuse response, not authentication.

Do not over-limit normal work
Rate limits need measurement. A payroll export, bulk upload, or autosaving UI can have
legitimate burst patterns; hardening must not silently become a reliability incident.

lessons.body:
Input Validation, Request Limits and
Injection Prevention
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Phase 12 remains the boundary
Zod server validation is now hardened with explicit maximum lengths, numeric ranges, enum allowlists and
strict object policies. Client validation is still UX only.

Allowlist reasoning
• Status/priority/sort are exact allowed values.

• Search/title/description have explicit maximum lengths.

• UUID/date fields use structured parsers rather than “dangerous character” blacklists.

• Request bodies and uploads have size limits before expensive processing.

• Unknown write fields remain rejected.

Injection prevention
Prisma parameterizes normal database values; do not bypass it with string-concatenated raw SQL. If raw
SQL is truly required, parameterize values and keep identifiers/operations on an allowlist.

Reject malformed content types
JSON endpoints should expect the intended media type and return 415/400 where appropriate rather than
trying to reinterpret arbitrary payload formats.

lessons.body:
XSS, Output Handling and Content Security TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026 React helps, but escape hatches matter • Render user text as text; React escapes ordinary string interpolation. • Treat dangerouslySetInnerHTML as a security-sensitive escape hatch. • If rich HTML becomes a product requirement, sanitize with a maintained HTML sanitizer before rendering. • Validate untrusted href/src protocols; do not assume a string URL is safe. • Avoid eval/new Function and dynamic script construction. Example // Safe default: rendered as text

{task.description}

// Security-sensitive: only after deliberate sanitization policy //
CSP is defense in depth CSP can reduce XSS impact, but it does not replace safe rendering. The primary defense remains framework escaping, safe sinks and sanitization for intentionally rich HTML.

lessons.summary: CORS, CSRF and Browser Trust Boundaries TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026 Match controls to credential transport Browser security boundaries Browser Next.js NestJS Postgres untrusted client SSR / cookies Bearer API authoritative data XSS threatens browser-held capabilities; CSRF threatens ambient credentials. lessons.body:
CORS, CSRF and Browser Trust
Boundaries
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Match controls to credential transport
Browser security boundaries

Browser                              Next.js                               NestJS                              Postgres
untrusted client                     SSR / cookies                          Bearer API                        authoritative data

XSS threatens browser-held capabilities; CSRF threatens ambient credentials.

The Nest API uses explicit Bearer tokens, so CORS is not authentication and cookies require separate CSRF reasoning.

TaskFlow decisions
• NestJS business API: explicit Authorization: Bearer token. A malicious site cannot make the victim browser
magically know that token; CSRF risk is lower than with ambient cookies, but XSS/token theft remains
serious.

• Next.js SSR/Supabase session: cookies are ambient browser credentials. Use Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite
policy as supported by the auth integration and apply CSRF reasoning to state-changing
cookie-authenticated endpoints.

• CORS only controls which browser origins may read/send cross-origin requests under browser rules. It
does not authenticate the caller.

• Never use GET for state-changing operations.

Fetch Metadata
For cookie-authenticated state-changing routes, Sec-Fetch-* checks can be an additional layer after
compatibility testing. They supplement, not replace, proper CSRF defenses.

lessons.body:
Authentication, Session and
Authorization Abuse
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Hardening the existing chain
Supabase JWT
-> verify signature
-> verify expected issuer
-> verify audience / expiry
-> map claims.sub -> User.authSubject
-> load Workspace Membership
-> permission + resource scope
-> business rule

Controls
• Short-lived access tokens and proper refresh/session behavior.

• No access/refresh tokens in logs, URLs or query keys.

• Cache clearing on logout from Phase 22.

• 404 scoping when revealing resource existence would leak tenant data.

• Every resource lookup remains authorization-scoped; frontend-hidden buttons are not controls.

• Sensitive role/membership changes require stronger permission checks and audit evidence.

Testing
Reuse Phase 28 to test missing/expired/wrong-project tokens, cross-workspace ID tampering, role escalation
attempts and stale-session edge cases.

lessons.body:
Secrets, Configuration and
Environment Separation
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Classify configuration
• Public: Supabase project URL / publishable browser key where intended.

• Secret: service-role key, database URLs, deployment credentials, signing/admin tokens.

• Environment-specific: production, staging and development must not silently share powerful credentials.

Rules
# Never commit real values
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY=
DATABASE_URL=

# Browser-exposed prefix is NEVER for server secrets
# NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY= <-- prohibited

Operational lifecycle
• Provision through deployment secret stores rather than source control.

• Rotate/revoke after suspected exposure.

• Prefer short-lived/dynamic credentials where the platform supports them.

• Do not print process.env or ConfigService values during debugging.

• Maintain a secret inventory: owner, purpose, environments, rotation/revocation path.

lessons.body:
File Upload and Storage Hardening
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Phase 27 gets an adversarial review
• Keep private bucket default.

• Authorize before issuing an upload intent or signed download.

• Server generates object paths; original filename is display metadata only.

• Allowlist business-required MIME/extensions; enforce maximum size at multiple layers.

• Do not trust browser Content-Type alone; add content/signature scanning when business risk requires it.

• Use PENDING/READY/DELETING states to recover cross-system failures.

• Consider antivirus/CDR for documents in higher-risk deployments.

Threat examples
• Huge files / decompression bombs consume capacity.

• Active HTML/SVG/script payload is served inline and executes.

• Attacker guesses another tenant path.

• Service-role key turns a private bucket into a global bypass.

Serving rule
Private files are downloaded only after application authorization and through short-lived signed access. Do
not expose raw predictable object URLs as authorization.

TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Preserve the authoritative boundary

Dependency, Supply Chain, Logging
and Error Hardening
TaskFlow - Full Stack Developer 2026

Dependency hygiene
• Keep lockfiles committed and reproducible.

• Run pnpm audit/advisory review, but triage exploitability rather than blindly upgrading everything.

• Track supported framework branches and security releases. Next.js 16 is Active LTS in this course
baseline.

• Use automated dependency alerts and review transitive-risk changes before production deployment.

Log safely
• Keep requestId, user/domain ID where policy allows, route, status and failure category.

• Never log passwords, access/refresh tokens, session cookies, service-role keys, database connection
strings or encryption keys.

• Sanitize user-controlled values before structured logs to prevent log-forging/format injection.

Errors
Public errors remain stable and minimally informative; internal logs contain diagnostic context. Do not return
stack traces, Prisma internals, SQL, filesystem paths, environment variables or secret material.

Debugging Workshop — Phase 29: Security Hardening

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
asset/trust boundary -> abuse case -> preventive control -> detection/logging -> test -> residual risk

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Security checklist with no threat model
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Trusting hidden buttons as protection
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 3 — Secrets printed to logs/build output

Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket
Pick one failure from this workshop and write a short incident note: symptom, scope, root cause, fix, verification, and prevention. This is the same communication pattern used in professional bug reports and production incident follow-ups.

lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Security Hardening

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 29 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Threat-model TaskFlow and apply layered controls for access control, input/output safety, headers, abuse, secrets, uploads, dependencies, and configuration.

Required artifact
Security baseline checklist plus concrete tests for the most important abuse cases.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can describe assets and attackers.
• Can test broken access control.
• Can audit secret exposure.
• Can explain defense in depth and residual risk.

Independent build sequence
1. List sensitive assets and trust boundaries before selecting mitigations.
2. Run an IDOR/broken-access-control test by changing resource IDs as another user.
3. Review all external input boundaries and confirm validation plus parameterized/ORM-safe persistence.
4. Review rendering/output paths for XSS assumptions and add sensible content/security headers.
5. Check secret locations, source control, logs, client bundles, CI, and deployment settings.
6. Add abuse controls where justified and write security regression tests for discovered cases.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 29: Security Hardening. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

# TaskFlow Phase 29 Security Hardening Snapshot

Reference artifacts for the production hardening pass. Keep these controls aligned with the real deployment topology and verify them with tests.

# TaskFlow security hardening checklist

## HTTP / browser
- HTTPS only in production
- security headers verified
- CORS exact origins, methods and headers
- CSP designed/tested for deployed Next.js app
- no state-changing GET endpoints

## Identity / authorization
- JWT signature + issuer/audience/expiry verified
- authSubject mapping unique
- resource queries tenant-scoped
- 401/403/404 behavior tested
- role escalation denied

## Input / output
- server Zod validation on every untrusted body/query/path
- lengths/ranges/enums bounded
- React text rendering by default

- Next.js Support Policy: https://nextjs.org/support-policy

# TaskFlow threat model

Assets: authentication sessions, tenant business data, attachments, secrets, authorization decisions, audit/log evidence, service availability.

Entry points: Next.js pages/actions, NestJS HTTP API, Supabase Auth, Realtime, Storage signed uploads/downloads, PostgreSQL, deployment configuration.

Representative abuse cases:
- stolen/replayed access token
- cross-workspace object ID tampering
- brute-force / request flooding
- XSS through user content
- CSRF against cookie-authenticated flows
- malicious/oversized upload
- service-role key leaked to browser/logs
- dependency vulnerability left unpatched

# Never prefix server secrets with NEXT_PUBLIC_.

# Phase 29 security test matrix

## Headers
- API emits expected security headers
- Next.js emits nosniff/referrer/frame policy

## Rate limiting
- burst beyond route policy -> 429
- trusted proxy configuration preserves intended client tracker

## Input / errors
- oversized title/search/body rejected
- unknown fields rejected
- public 500 contains no stack/SQL/secret

## Authentication / authorization
- missing/expired/wrong-project token -> 401
- cross-workspace ID -> scoped 404/deny
- MEMBER role escalation -> forbidden
